Pennsylvania property tax is set by counties, school districts and municipalities, and assessment appeals follow a statutory calendar.

What the official sources say

  • Any person aggrieved by an assessment (whether or not the value changed) or an interested taxing district may appeal to the county board of assessment appeals by written appeal on or before September 1, or an earlier-set date no sooner than August 1 if county commissioners exercise the option and give publication notice at least two weeks prior. (53 Pa.C.S. 8844(c)(1),(3); source)
  • Appeal must identify appellant, property location, owner, assessment, and a mailing address for hearing notice. (53 Pa.C.S. 8844(c); source)
  • Homestead/Farmstead exclusion reduces the assessed value of each qualifying homestead/farmstead by the same amount before school property tax is computed; only a primary residence is eligible. (Taxpayer Relief Act (Act 1 of Special Session 1 of 2006); 53 Pa.C.S. Ch. 85 Subch. F (cite not on page); source)
  • Homestead/farmstead exclusion application must be filed by the preceding March 1 for tax years beginning July 1 or January 1. (DCED page (statute cite not shown); source)
  • Property Tax/Rent Rebate: up to $1,000 standard rebate for people 65+, widows/widowers 50+, and people with disabilities 18+; household income must be $48,110 or less; standard rebate tiers $1,000 ($0-$8,550), $770 ($8,551-$16,040), $460 ($16,041-$19,240), $380 ($19,241-$48,110); supplement for Philadelphia, Scranton, Pittsburgh; deadline December 31, 2026 for current cycle. (DOR PTRR page (Taxpayer Relief Act / Senior Citizens Rebate and Assistance Act cite not on page); source)
  • Real Estate Tax Sale Law (Act of July 7, 1947, P.L. 1368, No. 542; 72 P.S. 5860.101 et seq.) section 501: an owner, heirs, lien creditor or other interested person may discharge tax claims and liens by paying the bureau the claim plus interest, other tax claims/judgments, accrued returned taxes, and record costs. (Act 542 of 1947 sec. 501 (72 P.S. 5860.501); source)
  • Upset sale date: bureau schedules sale no earlier than the second Monday of September and before October 1; sale may be adjourned. (Act 542 sec. 601(a) (72 P.S. 5860.601); source)
  • No owner-occupied property may be sold at upset sale unless the bureau gave the owner-occupant written notice at least 10 days before the sale by personal service by the sheriff or deputy (or person appointed by county commissioners). (Act 542 sec. 602(e)(3) (72 P.S. 5860.602(e)(3)) as extracted; source)

Pennsylvania homestead exclusion FAQ

How do I apply for the homestead exclusion?

File with your county assessment office. Filing dates and forms are set by the county.

What is the Pennsylvania homestead exclusion?

It is a reduction in the assessed value of a primary residence, applied before school property tax is calculated. The Department of Community and Economic Development explains that the Taxpayer Relief Act, Act 1 of Special Session 1 of 2006, signed on June 27, 2006, sends property tax reduction allocations to each school district, and the district passes the benefit through a homestead or farmstead exclusion.

Every qualifying homestead or farmstead in the district is reduced by the same amount. Only a primary residence is eligible, and most owner-occupied homes and farms can qualify. The state is also clear that homeowners are not guaranteed the exclusion unless an added income tax is approved by voter referendum or enough funds have been collected for the Commonwealth to make the allocations.

Which properties count as a homestead?

A homestead is a dwelling, with its parcel and other improvements, that an owner who is a natural person uses as a domicile. The statutory definition quoted by DCED has three branches.

  • A house or other dwelling primarily used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person. The land is left out if someone else owns the land under the dwelling.
  • A condominium or cooperative unit used as the domicile of a natural person who owns it, limited to the assessed value of that unit.
  • A dwelling where only part is used as the owner's domicile, in which case the homestead is the share of the property equal to that portion.

A farmstead is a different category: the buildings and structures on a farm of at least ten contiguous acres that are used mainly for commercial agriculture, and it applies only to farms that serve as an owner's domicile.

When is the application due?

For tax years that begin July 1 or January 1, the application must be filed by the preceding March 1. DCED adds that school districts must notify homeowners by December 31 each year if a property has not been approved or if its approval is about to expire, so a letter in late December is a signal to refile.

The March 1 date comes from Section 341 of Act 72 of 2004, and DCED states that the Governor cannot extend it by executive order. Only new legislation could change it. Forms come from the county assessment office, so call the assessor in the county where the house sits for the current application.

How do the state, Allegheny County and Philadelphia programs differ?

The statewide exclusion lowers school taxes, while other homestead programs come from local law. Allegheny County runs a separate Act 50 exclusion that applies to county tax purposes only. Philadelphia runs its own Homestead Exemption through its Department of Revenue, with a flat $100,000 reduction and a December 1 filing date.

Three homestead programs and their filing rules (sources: DCED, Allegheny County, City of Philadelphia)
ProgramWhat it reducesFiling date
State exclusion under Act 1 of 2006Assessed value used for school property taxMarch 1 before the tax year
Allegheny County Act 50 exclusionAssessment for Allegheny County tax onlySet by the county; ask Allegheny County Real Estate
Philadelphia Homestead Exemption$100,000 off the taxable assessed valueDecember 1 each year; October 1 for the bill to reflect it

What is Act 50 and who can use it?

Act 50 of 1998 lets local governments create their own homestead and farmstead exclusions. Allegheny County explains that Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional change in November 1997 to allow a homestead exclusion, the General Assembly passed the Homestead Property Exclusion Program Act in May 1998, and the Act was amended on October 31, 2000.

Under the law, school districts, counties, townships, boroughs and cities can each adopt an exclusion. A taxing body can do so without changing its tax structure, as long as it can cover the cost without raising real property taxes. Districts that shift toward an earned income tax and lower the real property tax must use the exclusions to deliver the cut, and in exchange they drop several small taxes such as the per capita, occupation and occupational privilege taxes.

  • County of the second class: Act 50 as amended lets the county adopt its own rules and procedures for the program in place of the usual state administrative section.
  • Other locations: ask the county assessor whether the school district, county or municipality has adopted an exclusion of its own.
  • Amounts: each taxing body sets its own figure, so a neighbor in a different district may see a different reduction.

What does Philadelphia require and allow?

Philadelphia says you qualify if you own the home and live in it as your primary residence, and a mortgage or delinquent taxes do not disqualify you. Most homeowners save up to $1,399 a year on the Real Estate Tax bill, according to the City, and approval carries forward each year while you keep owning and living in the property.

  • You reapply only if the deed changes, for example when you refinance or add or remove a co-owner.
  • Owners with a 10-year residential tax abatement are not eligible until it expires, and a removed abatement cannot be put back.
  • A conditional exemption of up to three years is available when your name is not on the deed, such as after an inheritance, a fraudulent deed or a rent-to-own purchase.
  • Applications can go through the Philadelphia Tax Center, by phone at (215) 686-9200, or by mail to the Department of Revenue.

A denial can be appealed to the Board of Revision of Taxes within 30 days of the date on the denial letter. If a property no longer qualifies, the owner must tell Revenue within 45 days.

What happens to the exclusion when you sell the house?

The benefit follows an owner who lives in the home, so a sale ends your claim and the buyer applies on a new deed. Philadelphia asks for a fresh application when the deed changes, so a new owner who plans to live there should file once the deed is recorded.

Property tax bills do not stop at settlement. Ask the county treasurer or tax claim office which installments are paid, and check with your settlement agent how the closing statement divides the current bill. If you stop living in the house before you sell, for example after moving out of an inherited home, tell the assessor, because the exclusion applies only to a primary residence. In Philadelphia an owner who stops qualifying has 45 days to notify Revenue.

What should a seller check before listing a Pennsylvania home?

Start with the assessment office record for your parcel and confirm whether an exclusion is on it. If none is listed and you live in the house, ask the assessor how the county treats a late filing, since the March 1 date is fixed by statute for the following tax year.

Next, ask the county treasurer for the current tax bill and the payment status of each installment, so the closing statement divides the bill correctly. If the house was inherited and the deed still names a deceased relative, Philadelphia's conditional exemption shows that title problems are recognized in the program, and the county assessor can say what proof applies where you are.

Finally, gather the paperwork a title company will ask for: the most recent school and county tax bills, any homestead approval letter, and any abatement papers. Having them ready keeps a small tax question from delaying settlement.

More questions about Pennsylvania Homestead Exclusion

Is the Pennsylvania homestead exclusion automatic?

No, you apply to the county assessment office, and the application must be filed by March 1 before the tax year begins. School districts notify owners by December 31 if a property is not approved or its approval is expiring.

Does a rental or second home qualify?

No, only a primary residence is eligible. A dwelling must be used as the domicile of an owner who is a natural person, and when only part of the dwelling is the owner's home, the homestead is limited to that part.

Can Pennsylvania extend the March 1 deadline?

No executive order can do it. DCED states that the March 1 date is set by Section 341 of Act 72 of 2004, and the Governor cannot extend it, so only a change in the law could move the date.

How much does the Philadelphia Homestead Exemption save?

It removes $100,000 from the assessed value used to compute Real Estate Tax, and the City says most homeowners save up to $1,399 a year. The final filing date is December 1, with October 1 recommended for early filers.

Who do I ask for the form in another county?

Ask the county assessment office. DCED says the county provides its own homestead and farmstead application, and the filing dates and amounts for your school district come from that office.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

A Pennsylvania deed is recorded with the county recorder of deeds, and realty transfer tax and a statement of value can apply.

What the official sources say

  • The 1% state realty transfer tax is generally due when a document transferring title is filed with the county Recorder of Deeds; payment is evidenced by a stamp or impression affixed to the document. (72 P.S. 8101-C et seq.; DOR RTT Q&A; source)
  • Recorders of Deeds and commissioners of records are agents for sale of RTT stamps; a statement of value (REV-183) in duplicate is filed with a document presented for recording or for tax stamps, specifying true full value and why the instrument is not taxable. (61 Pa. Code 91.114, 91.112; Form REV-183; source)
  • Quitclaim deeds are taxable like other deeds if there is an actual conveyance; correctional and confirmatory deeds without consideration are not taxable if conditions met; deeds from ground rents, easements, life estates have special valuation rules. (61 Pa. Code 91.164, 91.151, 91.152; source)
  • Transfers from a living trust: a transfer for no/nominal consideration from the settlor to trustee of a living trust is excluded from tax; transfers from an ordinary trust are fully taxable except to vested remainder beneficiaries; the recorder must be presented a copy of the trust agreement to grant the exemption. (61 Pa. Code 91.156; source)
  • PA realty transfer tax is imposed at 1 percent on the value of real estate (including contracted-for improvements) transferred by deed, instrument, long-term lease or other writing; grantor and grantee are jointly and severally liable. (72 P.S. 8102-C (per DOR page); 61 Pa. Code 91.111(a)-(b), 72 P.S. 8107-C authority; source)
  • 61 Pa. Code 91.111: state tax at 1% of value of realty; it is the joint and several legal duty of the parties to pay; the duty may be discharged as the parties agree without prejudice to the Commonwealth's rights. (61 Pa. Code 91.111 (authority 72 P.S. 8107-C); source)
  • State RTT is collected, often with an additional local realty transfer tax, by county Recorders of Deeds; Recorders remit the 1% to the Dept of Revenue; locals may share their RTT among school districts and municipalities. (DOR Realty Transfer Tax overview (no statute cite on page); source)
  • Exempt transfers per DOR include certain transfers among family members, to governmental units, between religious organizations, to shareholders or partners, to/from nonprofit industrial development agencies, deeds to burial sites, certain transfers in real estate companies and farms, and property passed by testate or intestate succession. (72 P.S. 8102-C exclusions; 61 Pa. Code 91.193 (not itemized on page); source)

Pennsylvania mortgage foreclosures go through county courts, and the property is sold at a sheriff sale.

What the official sources say

  • Act 6 (41 P.S. 403): before a residential mortgage lender may accelerate, commence foreclosure or take possession, it must give the debtor written notice at least 30 days in advance, by registered or certified mail to last known address and the mortgaged residence; notice must state the obligation, default, right to cure and amount, cure time, how ownership may be terminated, and transfer/refinance rights. Not required if the property is abandoned or voluntarily surrendered. (Act of Jan. 30, 1974, P.L. 13, No. 6, section 403 (41 P.S. 403); source)
  • Act 6 section 404 right to cure: debtor or anyone on his behalf, not more than three times in a calendar year, may cure at any time at least one hour before the start of bidding at a sheriff sale by tendering amounts due plus reasonable fees and costs; cure restores the debtor to the pre-default position. (41 P.S. 404 (Act 6 of 1974 section 404); source)
  • Pa.R.C.P. 1141(a): an 'action' under the mortgage foreclosure chapter means an action to foreclose a mortgage on any estate, leasehold or interest in land; it does not include an action to enforce personal liability. 1141(b): procedure follows the rules for civil action unless otherwise provided. (Pa.R.C.P. 1141; source)
  • Pa.R.C.P. 1142: foreclosure action may be brought only in a county in which the land or part of it is located. (Pa.R.C.P. 1142; source)
  • Official Note to Rule 1147: if the mortgage is a residential mortgage under Act 101, the complaint should aver compliance with Section 403 of Act 6 (41 P.S. 403). (Pa.R.C.P. 1147 Official Note; source)
  • Philadelphia Residential Mortgage Foreclosure Diversion pilot (2008): owner-occupied residential premises must be scheduled for a Conciliation Conference before the sheriff sale can occur; goal is early determination of eligibility for loan work-out programs; non-residential and non-owner-occupied sales proceed as scheduled. (First Judicial District General Court Regulation No. 2008-01; source)
  • Deficiency judgments: when real property is sold to the judgment creditor in execution proceedings for less than the judgment, the creditor seeking the balance must petition the court to fix fair market value; debtor is released to the extent of fair market value (less prior liens etc.); if creditor fails to petition within the six-month period (42 Pa.C.S. 5522), debtor may petition to have the judgment marked satisfied. (42 Pa.C.S. 8103(a),(c),(d); source)
  • Pa.R.C.P. 3191 lists Acts not suspended by execution rules, including Section 32 of the Act of May 16, 1923, P.L. 207 (Municipal Claim and Tax Lien Law), 53 P.S. 7293 'relating to right of redemption after sale', and the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, 72 P.S. 5860.101. (Pa.R.C.P. 3191(a)(2); 53 P.S. 7293; source)

What the official sources say

  • A statement of value (specifying true, full and complete value and reason not taxable) must be filed in duplicate with a document presented for recording unless value is specified in document and no exclusion claimed; not required for wills, conventional mortgages, etc.; familial-relationship exception if deed indicates relationship. (61 Pa. Code 91.112; source)
  • In a bona fide sale, value is total agreed consideration and includes liens existing before transfer and not removed thereby, whether or not assumed. (61 Pa. Code 91.132(a)-(b); source)
  • Value is computed value (assessed value x common level ratio) for judicial sales, foreclosure, tax sales, gifts/nominal consideration, and non-bona-fide-sale transfers. (61 Pa. Code 91.135, 91.131; source)
  • Document evidencing devise by will or intestate law, without or with nominal consideration, is not taxable; transfer under an option to purchase in a will is taxable. (61 Pa. Code 91.159(a), 91.193(b)(7); source)
  • Philadelphia: the tax is usually split evenly between buyer and seller but this is not a legal requirement; the City may collect 100% from either party; based on sale price or assessed value plus assumed debt. (Philadelphia city page (no code cite); source)
Selling in Pennsylvania?
We buy Pennsylvania houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What we could not confirm

  • The Philadelphia total rate is not confirmed on an opened page.

Pennsylvania closing costs FAQ

Who pays Pennsylvania transfer tax?

Liability is joint and several, so parties usually agree who pays in the sales contract.

What closing costs does a Pennsylvania home seller face?

The one charge written into Pennsylvania law for nearly every deed is the realty transfer tax, and it is usually the largest line a seller can predict in advance. Other charges, such as a loan payoff, agent compensation and title work, depend on your contract and your lender, so ask your settlement agent for a written estimate before you sign.

The Department of Revenue describes the state tax as 1 percent of the value of the real estate, including improvements contracted for, transferred by deed, instrument, long-term lease or other writing. County recorders of deeds collect it at recording, usually together with a local transfer tax set by the school district and municipality. That local piece is why a closing in one Pennsylvania town can cost far more in transfer tax than a closing in the next county over.

  • State realty transfer tax: 1 percent of value.
  • Local realty transfer tax: set by the municipality and school district, so it varies by address.
  • Recording fees: paid to the county, and in Allegheny County by a separate check from the transfer tax.

How much is the Pennsylvania realty transfer tax by place?

The combined rate turns on the property's location. Allegheny County says its transfer tax ranges from 2 percent to 5 percent of the total consideration, with 1 percent going to the state and the rest to the municipality and school district. Philadelphia lists 3.578 percent for the City plus 1 percent for the Commonwealth, a total of 4.578 percent.

The Allegheny County Real Estate Division publishes worked examples that show how the pieces stack. A $40,000 house in Shaler Township carries a 2 percent total, while the same price inside the City of Pittsburgh carries 5 percent. For a house elsewhere in the state, ask the county recorder of deeds for the municipality and school district rates that apply to the parcel.

Transfer tax on a $40,000 sale in two Allegheny County locations (source: Allegheny County Real Estate Division)
LayerShaler TownshipCity of Pittsburgh
State1% ($400)1% ($400)
Municipality0.5% ($200)3% ($1,200)
School district0.5% ($200)1% ($400)
Total2% ($800)5% ($2,000)

Who pays the transfer tax, the buyer or the seller?

Both sides are legally on the hook, and the contract decides who actually writes the check. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.111, paying the tax is the joint and several duty of the parties, and they may split it as they agree, though the Commonwealth keeps its rights against both.

Philadelphia describes the common habit directly: the tax is usually split evenly between buyer and seller, which is not a legal requirement. The City can collect 100 percent from either party, so a seller who agreed to pay half still has an interest in seeing the full amount paid at settlement. Read the transfer tax clause in your agreement of sale, because a buyer can offer to absorb it as part of negotiation.

What value is the tax calculated on?

In an ordinary arm's length sale, the tax base is the total agreed consideration paid or to be paid. Section 91.132 adds that liens existing before the transfer and not removed by it count toward value, whether or not the buyer assumes the debt.

Some transfers use a computed value instead. Under 61 Pa. Code 91.135 that covers foreclosure, judicial and tax sales, gifts or nominal-consideration transfers, exchanges for stock or partnership interests, and transactions that are not bona fide sales. Philadelphia explains the method: take the assessed value from the Office of Property Assessment, apply the common level ratio set each year by the State Tax Equalization Board, and multiply the result by the tax rate. Allegheny County notes that new common level ratio factors take effect each year on July 1.

Which transfers escape the tax?

Several categories are excluded, but the exclusion must be claimed on the paperwork. The Department of Revenue names certain transfers among family members, transfers to governmental units, between religious organizations, to shareholders or partners, and to or from nonprofit industrial development agencies, plus deeds to burial sites, certain farm and real estate company transfers, and property passed by will or intestate succession.

  • Spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, and siblings fall within the family exclusion in 61 Pa. Code 91.193, and Philadelphia asks for documentation of the relationship.
  • A devise by will or under intestate law, made for no or nominal consideration, is not taxable, but a transfer under an option to purchase in a will is taxable.
  • Philadelphia says transfer tax is still due if mortgages, liens or debts on the property are not paid at the time of transfer.
  • A sale by an estate to a buyer is taxable. Philadelphia gives the example of property willed to several people and then sold to one of them.

What paperwork and deadlines go with the tax?

A statement of value, filed in duplicate with the deed, is the key form. It states the true, full and complete value and, if you claim an exclusion, the reason the document is not taxable. Section 91.112 lets the parties skip it when the deed itself states the full value and no exclusion is claimed, and a familial transfer can skip it if the deed clearly states the relationship. Allegheny County calls its version PA form REV-183.

Philadelphia says the tax is due when the document is presented for recording, and acquirers must pay within 30 days of acquiring the real estate. Misrepresenting the transaction or failing to record it can bring penalties of up to 50 percent of the tax due. Paying by mail there takes three certified checks: one to the Recorder of Deeds, one to the City and one to the Commonwealth. In Allegheny County, expect one check for transfer tax and a separate one for recording fees.

How does this apply to an inherited or as-is Pennsylvania house?

A house you inherit can pass to you without transfer tax, but selling it afterward is an ordinary taxable sale. The exclusion in 91.159 covers the devise itself, not a later deed from you to a purchaser, so plan for the full state and local rate at closing unless another exclusion fits.

If heirs divide property among themselves, 91.159 also treats a division in kind as taxable only to the extent someone takes more than an undivided share, or pays consideration. A buyer who purchases an as-is, tenant-occupied or repair-heavy house pays the same percentage as any other buyer, because the tax follows the price and the liens, not the condition. Ask the county recorder of deeds for the current local rate before you agree on a net figure.

More questions about Pennsylvania Closing Costs

Does Pennsylvania charge a state transfer tax on every home sale?

Yes, the state tax is 1 percent of the value of the real estate, unless the transfer is excluded. Excluded transfers include certain family transfers and property passed by will or intestate succession, and the exclusion has to be claimed on the filing.

Is the Philadelphia transfer tax higher than the rest of Pennsylvania?

Philadelphia lists 4.578 percent in total, made up of 3.578 percent for the City and 1 percent for the Commonwealth. Allegheny County reports a range of 2 percent to 5 percent, so the City of Pittsburgh reaches the top of that range while smaller municipalities sit lower.

Can the buyer pay the whole transfer tax?

Yes, the parties may agree on who pays under 61 Pa. Code 91.111. The Commonwealth keeps its rights against both parties, so the deal terms in your contract with the buyer do not remove the seller's legal exposure if the tax goes unpaid.

Do liens on the house raise the taxable value?

Yes, in a bona fide sale the value includes liens that existed before the transfer and were not removed by it, whether or not the buyer assumes the underlying debt. Liens paid off at closing do not add to the value.

Where do I find the local rate for my address?

Call the recorder of deeds for your house's county. That office collects the state tax and the local tax together at recording and can name the municipal and school district rates for the parcel.

What the official sources say

  • If no bid equal to the upset price is received, the sale continues without further advertisement so the bureau may sell at private sale or petition court for an order to sell free and discharged of liens (judicial sale). (Act 542 sec. 605-610 (72 P.S. 5860.605, 5860.610); source)
  • Within 30 days of presentation of the consolidated return the court confirms sales nisi if regularly conducted; bureau must notify each owner by certified restricted-delivery mail within 30 days of the actual sale of the right to file objections within 30 days after confirmation nisi. (Act 542 sec. 607 and 607(a.1) (72 P.S. 5860.607); source)

What we could not confirm

Pennsylvania tax sales FAQ

Can I stop a tax sale?

Paying the delinquent amount or selling before the sale can pay the tax from the proceeds. Ask the county tax claim bureau for exact amounts.

How does a Pennsylvania tax sale work?

A Pennsylvania tax sale is a forced sale of real estate to collect unpaid real estate tax. Outside the first and second class counties, a county tax claim bureau runs it under the Real Estate Tax Sale Law, published by the legislature as Act 542 of 1947. Philadelphia, the only first class county, follows a different statute and court process, covered further down.

Under the 1947 law, a tax claim is a first lien on the parcel. The bureau gives the owner a one-year window to pay, then offers the property at an upset sale, and then, if no one bids the full upset price, can ask the court of common pleas for a judicial sale. Each step carries its own notice rules, and a defect in notice is the most common ground for an owner to object.

The upset price is the total the bureau must recover. It adds the Commonwealth tax liens, the claim being sold on, any other tax claims or judgments, current-year taxes, municipal claims such as water or sewer, and the record and sale costs (section 605). That is why a house with a small tax debt can still carry an upset price well above the original bill.

Which law applies in Philadelphia and which in the rest of the state?

The 1947 Real Estate Tax Sale Law covers counties other than the first and second class, and Philadelphia is the state's only first class county. Philadelphia instead uses the Municipal Claim and Tax Lien Law of 1923 (Act 153), which sends delinquent accounts through the Court of Common Pleas and the Sheriff's Office.

  • Tax claim bureau counties: a September upset sale, no redemption after the sale, and a deed from the bureau to the buyer.
  • Philadelphia: a petition and court order, a sheriff's auction, and a nine month redemption period after the sheriff's deed is acknowledged for most homes.
  • A judicial sale under either system clears the taxing bodies' liens, while the 1947 law lets recorded mortgages and ground rents survive an upset sale unless they were part of the upset price.

What are the steps and dates in a tax claim bureau sale?

The calendar is fixed by statute, so an owner who tracks it can usually see the sale coming a year ahead. The table lists the main steps in order.

Tax claim bureau sale steps under Act 542 of 1947 (section numbers refer to the Act)
StepRuleSection
Notice of claimMailed by July 31 each year; a one-year discharge period starts July 1308
Pay and stay off the advertisementPayment before July 1 of the following year removes the property from the sale list501
Upset sale dateNo earlier than the second Monday of September and before October 1; may be continued to year end601
Published and mailed noticeAt least 30 days before the sale, by newspaper and certified mail; posting at least 10 days before602
Owner-occupied homesPersonal service by the sheriff or an appointee at least 10 days before the sale601(a)(3)
Return to courtConsolidated return within 60 days; owner objections within 30 days after confirmation nisi607

Source: Pennsylvania General Assembly text of the Real Estate Tax Sale Law.

How can an owner stop a tax sale before it happens?

An owner can stop the sale by paying, by signing a payment agreement, or by selling the house and paying the bureau from the closing proceeds. The options the statute names are:

  • Pay in full before July 1 of the year after the notice of claim, which also keeps the address out of the advertisement. Paying after July 1 but before the sale still stops it, though the property may appear in the printed list (section 501).
  • Sign a stay agreement with the bureau before the sale: 25 percent of the amount due up front and the balance in no more than three installments within one year (section 603). Missing a payment lets the bureau proceed at a sale held at least 90 days after the default.
  • Ask for an extension of up to 12 more months for owner-occupied real estate, if the county commissioners have adopted that program. The schedule must have at least four payments, with a first payment no larger than 25 percent (sections 502.1 and 503.1).
  • Ask about deferral if every owner-occupant is 65 or older and household income falls within the state rent rebate limit, where the county has adopted it (section 504).

The discharge certificate the bureau issues after payment records the satisfaction, and the bureau must forward collected money to the taxing districts at least every three months (section 501).

What happens to the title after an upset sale?

The title passes to the buyer once the court confirms the sale and the buyer pays the bid, and the owner has no right to redeem after the actual sale (section 501(c)). The bureau signs a fee simple deed as trustee, and the buyer pays to record it (section 608).

An upset sale conveys title subject to recorded mortgages, claims, ground rents and Commonwealth tax liens that were not included in the upset price (section 609). A judicial sale is stronger: the court orders the property sold free and clear of tax claims, mortgages and liens, other than separately taxed ground rents, and the leftover proceeds go to the office the commissioners designate (section 612).

An owner cannot buy the property back at a judicial sale, a private sale or from the repository for unsold property (section 618(a)). The one opening is narrow: if a property stays unsold after the upset sale and still sits on the bureau docket, the bureau may accept full payment of all returned taxes, costs, penalties and interest, but not installments (section 618(a.1)). A landlord whose rental license a municipality revoked cannot bid at the sale (section 601(d)).

How is a Philadelphia sheriff sale different?

In Philadelphia the City petitions the court to foreclose on a tax or other municipal lien, and the court orders a sale at a sheriff's auction. The City's Department of Revenue sends a warning of risk of tax foreclosure to qualifying accounts that owe and have no payment agreement. Online bidding for sheriff sales runs through Bid4Assets.com/Philadelphia, which the Sheriff's Office launched as its auction search platform in October 2026.

The 1923 statute gives the owner of a property sold on a tax or municipal claim nine months from the acknowledgment of the sheriff's deed to redeem by paying the bid, deed costs, taxes paid, other charges, and interest at 10 percent a year (section 32(a)). A vacant property carries no redemption right, and a home counts as occupied only if one individual or family lived there continuously for at least 90 days before the sale and still does when the deed is acknowledged (section 32(c)).

Philadelphia also offers the Owner-occupied Payment Agreement, which can set payments as low as $0 a month for some owners. The City's guidance is to contact the Department of Revenue, or the law firm named in the notice, as soon as a tax sale notice arrives.

Can I sell a house that is headed for a tax sale?

Yes. An owner can sell at any point before the actual sale, and the unpaid tax, interest and costs come out of the seller's side of the closing. The practical limit is time, because the buyer must close and the bureau must receive payoff funds before the sale date.

  • Ask the county tax claim bureau for a written payoff that includes the claim, interest, other tax claims, accrued current taxes and record costs.
  • Give that figure to the closing agent so it is paid from the seller's proceeds and the bureau issues its certificate of discharge.
  • Check for municipal claims, such as water and sewer, that sit outside the bureau's tax claim but still ride along in the upset price.
  • In Philadelphia, request a water payoff at least 30 days before settlement and ask the Department of Revenue for the real estate tax balance.

A seller who is short on time can ask a cash buyer to close quickly, as long as the payoff and the deed recording fit inside the sale calendar.

More questions about Pennsylvania Tax Sales

Can I get my house back after a Pennsylvania tax sale?

In a county run by a tax claim bureau, no. The statute says there is no redemption after the actual sale, and an owner cannot buy the property back at a judicial or private sale. Philadelphia is the exception, where an owner of an occupied home can petition to redeem within nine months after the sheriff's deed is acknowledged.

When is the Pennsylvania upset sale held?

The bureau sets it no earlier than the second Monday of September and before October 1, and it may be adjourned or continued. If the sale is held by the end of the calendar year, no new notice is needed. Ask the county tax claim bureau for its published date.

How much notice must the owner get?

Notice comes in several forms. The bureau publishes the sale and mails certified notice at least 30 days ahead, posts the property at least 10 days ahead, and serves an owner-occupant personally at least 10 days ahead. An owner who objects after the sale has 30 days from confirmation nisi to file.

What does a payment agreement require?

A stay agreement under section 603 requires 25 percent of the total due and the rest in no more than three installments inside one year. A default lets the bureau list the property again at a sale held at least 90 days later.

Does selling the house before the sale clear the tax debt?

Yes, if the closing pays the full payoff. The bureau applies the money to the claim, issues a certificate of discharge and removes the property from the sale list. Ask the bureau for the exact figure, since interest and costs change as the sale date nears.
